Case study

Urban Company

Who’s Coming keeps the booker and her parent informed from payment until the professional is at the door.

TIME3 weeks
TOOLSFigma, paper sketches
PLATFORMMobile app
PROJECT TYPENextLeap graduation project · Solo · UX research and UI design
Hero screens
View presentation ↗View prototype ↗
Context

InstaHelp, Urban Company’s instant booking service.

Urban Company is India’s on-demand home-services marketplace, and I focused on InstaHelp, its instant booking service. This was my solo NextLeap graduation project, covering UX research and UI design over about 3 weeks.

Problem

After payment, Urban Company goes quiet.

When you book for your parents in another city, the app stops telling you what’s happening. 32 of 40 people I surveyed said their worry peaks while waiting for the professional to arrive.

32 of 40

What I found when I booked for my own parents in Delhi

The confirmation showed only “Payment successful” and the city.
The professional’s name, photo and rating were one screen deeper, and nothing said what was checked.
Live location wasn’t tracked, and an “Arriving in 60 mins” ad sat above the real arrival time.
Cancelling cost me ₹50.
Payment successful screen
₹50 cancel screen

Why it matters

Possible cost to Urban Company: more cancellations, more “where is my professional?” calls and fewer repeat bookings.

Process

Audit, research, direction, test.

1

Audited it myself

I booked InstaHelp for my parents in Delhi and compared it with Pronto and Snabbit. None gave a parent a way to follow the wait.

2

Researched

40 survey responses and 6 interviews. They confirmed 4 of my 8 assumptions and changed 2.

3

Chose a direction

I scored 3 ideas. Live status + family share won (22/25). I dropped “open door” because the booker is remote.

4

Tested sketches

I tested paper sketches with 5 people and revised each key screen.

Proposal

Who’s Coming.

It keeps the booker and her parent informed from payment until the professional is at the door.

🔗

Right after paying

The booker shares in one tap. Mom gets a WhatsApp link and needs no app.

⏱

While waiting

One status sentence and one arrival time, with “Mom has her link” as confirmation.

🛡

At the door

Mom checks the professional’s face and ID badge. The OTP unlocks only after she confirms.

📅

During and after

Mom sees the same timer, and help and SOS stay one tap away.

Why this way

32 of 40 people worried most while waiting, so the design fills that silence. Live location is off by default to respect the professional’s privacy.

Open prototype ↗
Result

Confidence rose from 2.5 to 4.3 out of 5.

I tested the linked prototype with 4 people.

2.5 to 4.3confidence out of 5
2 of 4finished both tasks without help
4 peoplesmall sample, so direction only

What I’d measure next

  • User: confidence after booking, among first-time bookers
  • Business: repeat booking rate within 60 days
  • Guardrail: provider cancellation rate

Next steps

  • Validate the door-check moment (only 2 of 40 raised it)
  • Build the delay and failed-ID states
  • Run more usability tests

Case studyMobile commerce

Getto

A tracking flow that answers “when” and “where” on one screen.

RoleUX/UI design intern
Timeline4 weeks
PlatformMobile app
ToolsFigma, AI-assisted wireframes
What I deliveredOrder tracking, live map, ETA, delivery instructions, secure handoff
View presentation ↗
Context

A fashion app that promises 60 minutes.

Getto is a quick-commerce fashion app built for Getto shoppers. During my UX/UI internship, I redesigned its mobile order tracking flow in Figma, with design reviews from mentors and stakeholders.

60 mindelivery promise
4 weeksredesign in Figma
4 changesto the core tracking flow
Problem

The tracking screen never answered two questions.

When will it arrive, and where is it right now? For a brand built on speed, each gap adds anxiety instead of trust.

No timestamps

Users couldn’t tell how fresh a status was.

Map too late

Live location appeared only in the final minutes.

No control

No way to leave delivery instructions or confirm a secure handoff.

The original screens, annotated

Process

Audit, benchmark, map, iterate.

1

Audited the flow

There were no real users or live data, so I built the case from what I could verify. Findings are audit observations, not tested.

2

Benchmarked leaders

I rated Blinkit, Zomato, Swiggy and Uber Eats against Getto on six tracking criteria, from my own review. Getto rated lower on most.

3

Mapped the journey

Across 7 stages, I hypothesised that confidence dips during “preparing” and “out for delivery,” where information is thinnest.

4

Structured the flow

I grouped content into six clusters so nothing critical is more than one tap away, and merged ETA and live location into one screen.

5

Iterated wireframes

I moved from a flat status card to a hierarchy that leads with the ETA.

Proposal

“When” and “where” on one screen.

One decision drove everything: ETA and live location come first, and every other module supports them.

⏱

ETA first

“Arriving in 56 mins” leads the screen, with no scrolling.

📍

Live map immediately

Location shows from the first tracking screen, not only near arrival.

📝

Delivery instructions

A persistent slot with one-tap options (leave at door, don’t ring bell) and free text for edge cases.

🔐

Secure handoff

An OTP module with “don’t share before delivery arrives,” plus a rider card showing photo, name, rating and a call button.

One status card, five stages

One status card is reused across all five stages, so every update reads instantly. Status uses colour, icon and text, never colour alone, and tap targets are at least 44px.

Before vs after

Key tracking screens

Remaining screens and components

Result

What I’d expect, and how I’d test it.

This project stayed internal and didn’t reach real users, so these are expected outcomes, not measured results.

Expected outcomes

  • Faster time to understand order status
  • ETA easier to find and plan around
  • Earlier visibility of delivery location
  • More control through delivery instructions

What I learned

  • In time-sensitive flows, layout order is the feature. Hierarchy matters more than any one screen’s polish.
  • Showing the right information at the right moment reduces uncertainty more than showing more.

Next steps

Test with real users and measure time to find the ETA and task completion for adding delivery instructions.

“Getto’s tracking flow didn’t need more information. It needed the right information, in the right order, at the right moment.”

Case studyAI product

OpsPilot

An AI workspace that shows evidence before sensitive actions.

My roleUI/UX Designer
Time3 weeks
PlatformWeb app
Built forTeams operating AI agents
ToolsFigma, Lovable
TypeConcept project
View live prototype ↗
Context

A concept workspace for AI agents.

OpsPilot is a concept workspace for managing AI agents that do real operational work and pause for human approval on sensitive actions. I designed the UX and product structure in Figma and built a working prototype in Lovable.

3 weeksconcept project
6 statesfor every agent and task
4 areasDashboard, Approval, Task run, Audit History
Problem

Most AI products are built to feel autonomous.

When an agent acts on money or customers, operators can’t see what it is doing or who decided what happened.

₹4,999duplicate charge, above the Refund Assistant’s ₹1,000 limit. It must stop and give a human the evidence.

Four pain points

Silent automation

Alert fatigue

Decisions without context

Every failure treated the same

Process

Research, map, decide, define.

1

Researched

I compared GitHub Actions, PagerDuty and Zapier on approvals, failures and audit history. Finding: separate “Approval required” from “Needs attention.”

2

Mapped the flow

Task, agent run, human handoff, completion. The handoff is where trust is won or lost, so I designed around it.

3

Made one key call

I skipped separate Tasks and Approvals lists, because the dashboard already shows everything pending.

4

Defined six states

Running, Idle, Paused, Waiting for approval, Flagged, Completed.

Proposal

One question on every screen.

An operator workspace where every screen answers one question: what is the agent doing now, or who decided what happened.

Audit History

Records every decision.

Six states

RunningIdlePausedWaiting for approvalFlaggedCompleted

Each has a colour and a label.

Open live prototype ↗
Result

A structured review, not user testing.

No usability testing and no metrics. I validated the design with a structured prototype review.

What changed after the review

  • The ₹4,999 refund now shows first under “Needs your attention.”
  • Evidence is separate from the Approve/Reject buttons.
  • A paused task keeps its progress (“5 of 6 cases reviewed”).
  • Status badges match between list and detail views.

Next

Test whether operators can find and understand the Approval screen from the dashboard.
